slides.headline: A $1,999 MacBook Pro With an Awkward Pitch
slides.subheadline: The M6 improves performance, but mandatory storage and missing flagship features complicate the upgrade.

slides.headline: What the M6 Upgrade Actually Delivers

items.title: Measured gains over M5
items.body: CPU improvements: around 7 percent and 15 percent for single- and multi-core performance, respectively.

items.title: A bigger performance jump
items.body: GPU performance improves between 20 and 30 percent over M5, depending on the test.

items.title: Ports remain a selling point
items.body: Three Thunderbolt 4 ports across both sides; dedicated HDMI, SD card reader, MagSafe, headphone jack.

slides.headline: The Pro Advantage Beyond the Chip

left.title: Brighter display, active cooling
left.description: 14.2 inches; Mini LED; 120 Hz; 1,000 nits maximum SDR; up to 1,600 nits HDR.

right.title: Thinner, lighter, fanless
right.description: 13.6- and 15.3-inch displays use 60 Hz IPS screens; both comparison models lack cooling fans.

metrics.label: INCREASE OVER M1
metrics.context: Compared with the basic M1 MacBook Pro from 2020.

metrics.label: INCREASE OVER M5
metrics.context: Compared with the M5 MacBook Pro's starting price a year ago.

slides.quote: It’s an exciting year for the MacBook Pro! Just not for this MacBook Pro.
slides.role: Reviewer, according to the supplied byline
slides.context: The reviewer contrasts this entry-level refresh with newer flagship models.

slides.headline: The Configuration Catches Behind the Price

items.title: No smaller storage choice
items.body: The 1TB allotment is mandatory, even for buyers who do not need it.

items.title: Matte costs more
items.body: The optional nano-texture matte display upgrade adds $150 to the $1,999 starting price.

items.title: Base RAM remains 16GB
items.body: 24GB and 32GB upgrades are available; the reviewer identifies RAM as the biggest limitation for running models.

items.title: Memory capacity changes bandwidth
items.body: 16GB receives 153 GB/s; 24GB and 32GB configurations receive 170 GB/s.

slides.headline: New Silicon Does Not Mean New Design

left.title: $1,999 buys the newest flagship features
left.description: Assuming the M6 name guarantees Apple's latest display and chassis technology.

right.title: The design dates to 2021
right.description: No touchscreen, OLED panel, Dynamic Island, half-pound weight reduction, or glowing Apple logo.

slides.headline: Buy for Specific Features, Not the Badge

avoid.title: Buyers expecting more
points: Skip if $1,999 must buy Apple's newest OLED touchscreen and flagship design features.
Question the mandatory 1TB and $500 to $700 upgrade over the 13- or 15-inch MacBook Air.
M4 or M5 owners: the reviewer expects improvement, but likely not a staggering difference.

fit.title: Buyers with clear priorities
points: The reviewer calls this Apple's cheapest laptop option for 120 Hz ProMotion or the optional $150 nano-texture finish.
Choose for HDMI, an SD card reader, and three Thunderbolt 4 ports distributed across both sides.
M1 or M2 MacBook Air or Pro owners: the reviewer expects a sizable everyday improvement.
For sustained workloads, the reviewer expects active cooling to retain an advantage over a prospective fanless M6 Air.

slides.headline: Do Not Mistake Expectations for Announcements

items.title: An M6 refresh is anticipated
items.body: The reviewer expects an M6 MacBook Air; no confirmed configuration or release date is supplied.

items.title: The wait is speculative
items.body: The reviewer would not be surprised by at least two years before this tier receives an OLED touchscreen.

items.title: Rumor is not a commitment
items.body: Suggestions that M6 will lack Pro, Max, or Ultra configurations are explicitly presented as rumor.

slides.headline: A Capable Laptop. A Difficult Value Argument.
slides.verdict: Best suited to buyers prioritizing 120 Hz ProMotion, extra ports, and active cooling—not Apple's newest flagship features.
slides.question: Are those advantages worth $500 to $700 over the 13- or 15-inch MacBook Air?
slides.actionText: Where do you draw the line?
